gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much power each 120 V leg gets when a split-phase power station feeds a transfer switch through its L14-30 port. Anker says the F3800 Plus's 6,000 W L14-30R is a 25 A port, which works out to 3,000 W per leg, and its TT-30R only gets power from leg L1. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3's 4,000 W total over 240 V works out to about 2,000 W per leg, and it runs its 120 V inverter or its 240 V inverter, not both at once.
standout_why: I read three of the results ChatGPT got: two itechguides pages (both cited) and outagereadyhq (cited). outagereadyhq lists amp ratings for the transfer switches and total watts for the Jackery 5000 Plus (7,200 W) and Anker S5000 (4,500 W), but gives no per-leg wattage or amps. itechguides' sizing page gives the DELTA Pro Ultra's 7,200 W as a total only. itechguides' buying guide gives cycle life to 70% for small Jackery units only, gives Anker S2000 cycles with no end point, and says nothing about 240 V beyond 'confirm split-phase'. None of them gives cycle life for the large home-backup units with the capacity end point attached. I did not open calcpanel, the ankersolix blog or the PG&E PDF.
decides: Through a transfer switch most house loads (fridge, furnace blower, sump pump, microwave) are 120 V, and each one sits on one leg. So the per-leg figure, not the headline wattage, decides whether a fridge plus a microwave on the same leg trips the unit. On per-leg power the F3800 Plus (3,000 W per leg) beats the DELTA Pro 3 (about 2,000 W per leg), even though the DELTA Pro 3's 4,000 cycles to 80% is the only cycle-life figure I sourced with its end point. Anker gives the F3800 Plus as '3,000+ cycles' and the S5000 as '10,000 cycles', with no end point for either, so as published those two counts cannot be compared with EcoFlow's.
